case.display_title: Two weeks of bleeding gums and nosebleeds

source.title: Superwarfarin Rodenticide Poisoning due to Consumption of Exotic Animals: A Case Report

clock.semantics: Integer day relative to admission. day = null means the fact is valid at any point in the admission (the article gives no date).

vignette: A 37-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and chronic hepatitis B on tenofovir presents with two weeks of intermittent bleeding from the gums and nose and two days of blood in his urine.
opening_statement_lay: For two weeks my gums and my nose keep bleeding, on and off, and for the last two days there's been blood in my urine. The tablets the dentist gave me didn't help.

facts.release_text: 37-year-old man, originally from China, who has lived in the United States for 15 years.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus, poorly controlled. Chronic hepatitis B, treated with tenofovir.
Intermittent bleeding from the gums and nose for two weeks.

facts.item: Presenting complaint: blood in the urine
facts.release_text: Blood in the urine for two days.

Seen by his primary care physician two weeks ago and referred urgently to gastroenterology for a suspected bleeding lesion of the upper gastrointestinal tract. After the endoscopy he was referred to a dentist, who prescribed oral tranexamic acid for two days, without improvement. The blood in the urine began after that.
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy before admission: no oesophageal or gastric bleeding; bleeding was seen in the oral cavity.
No recent illness, and no contacts with similar symptoms.
Worried that the bleeding is related to drinking alcohol at a party several weeks ago.
No previous bleeding problems: no earlier bleeding from the mouth or nose, no excessive bleeding after injuries or surgery, and no episodes of joint swelling and pain.
Takes no anticoagulant (blood-thinning) medicine, and no family member takes warfarin.
facts.source_locator: Case study; Discussion of the work-up

facts.release_text: Current tobacco smoker.
Drinks alcohol occasionally.
Eats mostly leftover meats, with very few vegetables or fruit.
Works as a chef in a Chinese restaurant.
Returned two months ago from a month-long trip to China.
His sister has systemic lupus erythematosus. No family history of bleeding disorders.
Lives with his sister.

facts.item: Rat poison at home or work
facts.release_text: Firmly denies using rat poison at home or at work; there have been no problems with rats or mice at either place.

facts.item: Unusual foods eaten abroad (hidden until asked specifically)
facts.release_text: While in China he ate rodents and other exotic animals bought at a street market.

release_condition.note: A general diet question returns H13 only, and a toxin or pesticide question returns H18. In the article he recalled eating rodents only on further questioning, after the rodenticide panel was positive.

facts.release_text: Dried blood on the lips and at the left nostril, with some oozing from both sites.
Blood pressure 106/71 mmHg; pulse 86/min; temperature 36.6 °C; respiratory rate 16/min; SpO2 96%.

series.note: Day 0: 'incalculably high INR' with PT 112 s (text; not plotted in Figure 2). Day 11: the discharge value, 2.04 in the text and the last point of Figure 2 ('Day 11 at 5:00').

Read from the figure image (data labels). Figure 2 plots 18 INR results against 'Day N at time'; figure Day N is taken as case day N (admission, day 0, carries the unplotted incalculable INR). One point per day: the day's last reading. All readings: Day 1 at 12:00 p.m. 7.00; Day 1 at 7:00 p.m. 8.57; Day 2 2:00 a.m. 3.37; Day 3 at 4:00 a.m. 6.31; Day 4 at 1:00 p.m. 5.36; Day 4 at 7:00 p.m. 3.28; Day 5 1:00 a.m. 2.37; Day 5 2:00 a.m. 7.11; Day 6 at 3:00 a.m. 7.23; Day 6 at 7:00 p.m. 2.51; Day 7 at 3:30 a.m. 4.34; Day 7 at 10:30 3.96; Day 7 at 8:30 p.m. 2.37; Day 8 at 1:30 a.m. 1.90; Day 8 at 3:00 p.m. 2.27; Day 9 at 2:00 a.m. 2.03; Day 10 at 5:30 a.m. 1.91; Day 11 at 5:00 2.04.

media.redacted_caption: Times at which results were reported, by sequence number.

gaps.guidance: Not reported. PT follows Figure 2's INR; APTT falls unevenly from 112 s and is normal by discharge.
Day 11: Figure 2's last point ('Day 11 at 5:00') is the discharge INR of 2.04.

gaps.item: Blood count indices and later counts
gaps.guidance: Normocytic anaemia of blood loss; slow recovery without transfusion.
Poorly controlled type 2 diabetes: metformin with poor adherence; raised glucose and HbA1c; glycosuria.
HBsAg and anti-HBc reactive; well suppressed on tenofovir; no cirrhosis.
Partial rise of II, VII, IX and X, in step with the INR.

gaps.item: Examination beyond the mouth and nose
gaps.guidance: Pallor; oozing gums; bruising at venepuncture sites; no stigmata of chronic liver disease; no haemarthrosis; no neurological signs.
Macroscopic haematuria with glycosuria on admission, clearing by day 5; normal renal tract imaging.

final_diagnosis.text: Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide (brodifacoum) poisoning, most likely from eating rodents or other animals bought at a street market in China, causing an acquired vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy with gum and nose bleeding and haematuria

secondary_findings: Anaemia (haemoglobin 72 g/L) from two weeks of mucosal bleeding and haematuria
Poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (raised glucose and HbA1c, glycosuria)
Chronic hepatitis B, suppressed on tenofovir, without cirrhosis: not the cause of the coagulopathy (factor V and fibrinogen normal)
accepted_differential: Vitamin K deficiency from poor diet or malabsorption
Coagulopathy of liver disease (chronic hepatitis B)
Acquired haemophilia or another acquired factor inhibitor
Congenital factor deficiency or von Willebrand disease
Deliberate self-poisoning or poisoning by another person
Haemorrhagic fever with renal involvement after travel (for example dengue, leptospirosis)
red_herrings: alcohol at a party several weeks earlier
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and dental referral
key_discriminators: PT and APTT both 112 s with an unmeasurable INR
factors II, VII, IX and X very low with factor V normal
partial and unstable response to 10 mg doses of vitamin K
no anticoagulant medicine in the home
rodents eaten at a street market abroad
ground_truth.treatment_given: Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg: four doses over 48 hours, then 13 more doses during the admission; bleeding stopped, APTT normalised and the INR fell to 2.04 at discharge. Discharged on oral vitamin K 100 mg daily with haematology follow-up for INR monitoring.
ground_truth.outcome: INR labile between 1.00 and 1.91 over the next three months; 0.94 four months after discharge on oral vitamin K 100 mg daily. No further bleeding.
must_do: Give vitamin K promptly (intravenously while bleeding) for bleeding with a markedly prolonged PT and APTT
Define the defect: vitamin K-dependent factor assays (II, VII, IX, X) with factor V as the control, or at least a mixing study
Ask about anticoagulant medicines and rat poison at home and at work
Send an anticoagulant rodenticide panel when no warfarin exposure explains a vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency
Take a detailed travel and dietary history, including unusual foods eaten abroad
Plan months of high-dose oral vitamin K with regular INR checks after discharge
Involve haematology in the work-up and long-term follow-up
must_not_do: Treat the bleeding with tranexamic acid alone, without vitamin K
Discharge without long-term high-dose vitamin K once the INR first improves (long-acting rodenticides persist for months)
Order a liver or kidney biopsy while the coagulopathy is uncorrected
Start anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs, including pharmacological thromboprophylaxis
Conclude deliberate self-poisoning without first taking a full dietary and travel history

diagnosis_rubric_anchors.5: Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning, with eating animals bought at a street market abroad identified as the likely source
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.4: Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning, source not identified
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.3: Vitamin K deficiency coagulopathy without naming a long-acting anticoagulant
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.2: Coagulopathy of liver disease, DIC, acquired haemophilia, warfarin over-anticoagulation or deliberate self-poisoning as the final diagnosis
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.1: Unrelated diagnosis, or one that would lead to harm

teaching_points: A prolonged PT and APTT with normal platelets, fibrinogen and D-dimer, and low factors II, VII, IX and X with a normal factor V, is the signature of vitamin K deficiency or antagonism rather than liver disease or DIC.
When no warfarin is involved, a long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide is the leading cause; test for it and ask again about exposure, including food.
Long-acting rodenticides persist for months: standard vitamin K doses give an incomplete, unstable response, and treatment needs high-dose oral vitamin K for months with INR monitoring.
Rodenticides accumulate in the food chain: eating rodents, or animals that prey on them, is a possible route of exposure.
